title: Of Cato the Younger
paragraphs: ["I am not possessed by this common error of judging others by what I am myself. I easily believe things in others that differ from me. Though I am bound to one form, I do not tie the world to it, as every man does. I believe and conceive a thousand ways of living contrary to the common one." — Florio, ed. 1613, p. 113.]

I am not guilty of the common error of judging another by myself. I easily believe in someone else a temperament opposite to my own; and though I find myself committed to one particular way, I do not bind others to it as so many do. I believe in and grasp a thousand contrary ways of life, and, unlike most people, I more readily accept difference than uniformity among us. I will, as openly as anyone could wish, release a man from my own moods and principles and consider him on his own terms. Though I am not continent myself, I sincerely approve the continence of the Feuillants and Capuchins and praise their way of life highly. I imagine myself into their place, and love and honour them all the more for being unlike me. I very much want each of us to be judged on his own, and not dragged into the implications of common examples. My own weakness does not at all diminish the esteem I owe to the strength and vigour of those who deserve it:
"Sunt qui nihil suadent, quam quod se imitari posse confidunt."
["There are those who recommend nothing except what they think they can themselves imitate." — Cicero, De Orator., c. 7.]

Crawling along on the slime of the earth, I do not for that reason stop watching, up in the clouds, the unreachable height of certain heroic souls. It is a lot for me to have my judgment sound and just, even if my actions cannot be; to keep this sovereign part, at least, free from corruption. It is something to have my will right and good even where my legs fail me. This age we live in, in our part of the world at least, has grown so dull that not just the practice but even the very imagination of virtue is faulty, and seems to be no more than college jargon:
"Virtutem verba putant, ut Lucum ligna:"
["They think virtue is mere words, as they think a sacred grove is mere wood." — Horace, Ep., i. 6, 31.]
"Quam vereri deberent, etiam si percipere non possent."
["Which they ought to reverence, even if they cannot comprehend it." — Cicero, Tusc. Quas., v. 2.]

It has become a trinket to hang in a cabinet or to dangle from the tongue, like an earring, for show only. There are no longer any virtuous actions to be found; those that have the look of virtue still have none of its essence, because profit, glory, fear, custom, and other such external causes are what put us up to producing them. Our justice too, our courage, our courtesy, can be called by those names — but only as they appear to others and present themselves to the public. In the doer they cannot be virtue, since there is another end in view, another moving cause. Now virtue acknowledges nothing as her own except what is done by herself and for herself alone.

In the great battle of Plataea, which the Greeks under Pausanias won against Mardonius and the Persians, the victors, when dividing the glory of the action according to their custom, gave the Spartan nation the highest credit for valour in the engagement. The Spartans, expert judges of virtue, came to decide which particular Spartan deserved the honour of having behaved best on that occasion. They found that Aristodemus had risked himself with greater bravery than any other; but they would not award him the prize, on the grounds that his courage had been driven by a wish to clear his name of the disgrace he had earned at Thermopylae and to die well so as to wipe out that earlier stain.

Our judgments are still sick, and obey the temper of our corrupt manners. I notice that most of the wits of these times claim cleverness by trying to tarnish and darken the glory of the bravest and most generous deeds of former ages, putting some mean interpretation on them and inventing trivial causes and motives for the noble things they did. A great subtlety, indeed! Give me the greatest and least blemished action the world has ever seen and I will dream up a hundred plausible aims and ends to discredit it. God knows, if you draw them out fully, what range of motives our inner wills are open to. They don't so much play the censor maliciously as practise their detractions ignorantly and crudely.

The same effort and licence others spend on smudging and slandering these illustrious names, I would gladly take up to lend them my shoulder and raise them higher. These rare figures, picked out by the consensus of the wisest men of all ages as examples for the world, I would not hesitate to magnify in honour, as far as my invention would allow, by every favourable interpretation; and we may well believe that the force of our imagination falls infinitely short of their merit. It is the duty of good men to picture virtue as beautifully as they can; and there would be nothing wrong if our passion carried us a little away in favour of so sacred a form. What these other people do, on the contrary, they do either out of malice or from the vice of limiting their belief to their own capacity — or, what I am more inclined to think, because their eyes are not strong, clear, and lifted enough to take in the splendour of virtue in her native purity. Plutarch complains that in his own time some put the cause of the younger Cato's death down to fear of Caesar, at which he is rightly indignant; from which one can gather how much more offended he would have been with those who attributed it to ambition. Senseless people! Cato would rather have done a noble, just, and generous deed and been rewarded with disgrace than with glory. That man was, in truth, a pattern nature chose to show how high human virtue and constancy could reach.

But I am not equal to handling so rich a subject, and so I will only line up five Latin poets in competition praising Cato — and, incidentally, themselves. Now, a well-educated child will find the first two, compared with the others, a little flat and faint; the third more vigorous, but overdone by the extravagance of his own force. He will then judge there is room for one or two more steps of invention to reach the fourth, and on reaching that he will raise his hands in admiration. Coming to the last, separated by some distance from the first (a distance he will swear no human wit can fill), he will be astonished, he will not know where he is.

And here is the wonder: we have far more poets than judges or interpreters of poetry. It is easier to write it than to understand it. There is, indeed, a certain low and middling sort of poetry that can be judged by set rules of art; but true, supreme, divine poetry is above all rules and reason. Whoever discerns its beauty with the surest and steadiest sight sees no more than the quick flash of a lightning bolt: it does not exercise the judgment but ravishes and overwhelms it. The fury that possesses the man capable of penetrating it wounds a third person too, by hearing him recite it — like a magnet that not only draws the needle but also gives the needle the power to draw others. And it is even more clearly visible in our theatres: the sacred inspiration of the Muses first stirs the poet to anger, sorrow, hatred, or whatever they please, beyond himself; through the poet it then possesses the actor, and through the actor in turn, all the spectators. That is how our passions hang upon and depend on one another.

Poetry has had this power over me from childhood, to pierce me through and carry me away; but this vivid feeling, natural to me, has been handled differently by different forms — not so much higher or lower (since they were always the highest of their kind) as different in colour. First, a gay and sprightly fluency; then a lofty and penetrating subtlety; and finally a mature and steady vigour. Their names will say it better: Ovid, Lucan, Virgil.
But our poets are beginning their race:
"Sit Cato, dum vivit, sane vel Caesare major,"
["Let Cato, while he lives, be considered greater than Caesar himself." — Martial, vi. 32]
says one.
"Et invictum, devicta morte, Catonem,"
["And Cato unconquered, conquering death itself." — Manilius, Astron., iv. 87.]
says the second. And the third, speaking of the civil wars between Caesar and Pompey:
"Victrix causa diis placuit, sed victa Catoni."
["The victorious cause pleased the gods, the defeated one pleased Cato." — Lucan, i. 128.]
And the fourth, on the praises of Caesar:
"Et cuncta terrarum subacta, Praeter atrocem animum Catonis."
["And all the earth subdued, except the unyielding mind of Cato." — Horace, Od., ii. 1, 23.]
And the master of the choir, after parading all the great names of the greatest Romans, ends with this:
"His dantem jura Catonem."
["Cato giving laws to all the rest." — Aeneid, viii. 670.]
